questions.q: What question does SQL Auditing answer that TDE, Always Encrypted, DDM, RLS, and classification cannot answer by themselves?
options: "Who accessed this specific table, and when, and what did they do?" — a historical record of actual activity, not a rule about what's currently allowed
"Is this column encrypted at rest?"
"What sensitivity label is applied to this column?"
"Which rows can this user currently see?"
questions.explain: The other tools shape what's protected and how; auditing produces the historical record a compliance investigation actually needs.

questions.q: Where does SQL Auditing write its captured events, and why not inside the audited database itself?
options: To a Storage account, Log Analytics workspace, or Event Hub — kept outside the database so the audited principals can't alter the record of their own activity
Directly into the audited table's own transaction log, for simplicity
Into a temporary table that is dropped after each session ends
Auditing does not persist any data anywhere; it is real-time only
questions.explain: A tamper-resistant destination is core to making the audit record actually defensible in a compliance investigation.

questions.q: What is the difference between a server audit specification and a database audit specification?
options: A server audit specification covers server-wide events like logins and role changes; a database audit specification targets database-specific events like SELECT/UPDATE on named tables
They are identical, just named differently for legacy reasons
A database audit specification can only audit schema changes, never data access
A server audit specification cannot write to a storage account, only to Log Analytics
questions.explain: Targeting a database audit specification at already-classified sensitive tables turns generic logging into a directly compliance-relevant control.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what makes an audit log a real compliance control rather than just a technical feature turned on?
options: Being enabled and correctly scoped, written to a tamper-resistant destination, retained long enough to matter, and actually reviewed by someone
Simply having STATE = ON set on the server audit, regardless of anything else
Using the default storage account retention settings
Auditing every single event type indiscriminately across every table
questions.explain: An audit log nobody ever queries is described in this lesson as a compliance liability, not a control.

questions.q: Why can't Row-Level Security or Dynamic Data Masking answer "who accessed this table last Tuesday," even though both control access to that table?
options: Because they control what a query is currently allowed to see or return, not a historical record of past activity — that requires SQL Auditing's event logging
Because RLS and DDM are only available on Managed Instance, not Azure SQL Database
Because RLS and DDM automatically disable themselves after one week
Because auditing is a prerequisite that must be enabled before RLS or DDM can function at all
questions.explain: Access-control features and audit logging solve different problems — current behavior vs. historical proof.
